courses.title: Discrete Mathematics and Graph Theory
courses.tagline: Reason about finite structures, prove what must be true, and turn graph models into efficient algorithms.

modules.title: Counting principles
modules.definition: The product rule multiplies the number of choices made in sequence. The pigeonhole principle guarantees repetition when more objects are placed into fewer boxes. Inclusion-exclusion corrects double counting across overlapping sets.
modules.equation: |A union B| = |A| + |B| - |A intersection B|
modules.example: A system generates a two-letter code followed by one digit. There are 26 x 26 x 10 = 6,760 possible codes. If 11 requests are assigned to 10 servers, at least one server receives two requests.
modules.checkpoint: Can you identify whether a problem needs the sum rule, product rule, pigeonhole principle, or inclusion-exclusion?

modules.title: Recurrences and generating functions
modules.definition: A recurrence defines each term using earlier terms. A generating function encodes a sequence as coefficients of a formal power series, allowing algebraic manipulation of the whole sequence.
modules.example: For binary strings with no consecutive 1s, let a_n be the count at length n. Splitting on the last bit gives a_n = a_(n-1) + a_(n-2), with a_1 = 2 and a_2 = 3.
modules.checkpoint: Write base cases before expanding or solving a recurrence.

modules.title: Logic, sets, languages and machines
modules.definition: Logic formalizes valid inference; set theory describes collections and operations. A formal language is a set of strings over an alphabet. A finite state machine accepts a string by following transitions from a start state to an accepting state.
modules.equation: p implies q is equivalent to (not p) or q
modules.example: A two-state machine can accept binary strings ending in 1: state q0 means the current suffix ends in 0 or is empty; q1 is accepting and means it ends in 1.
modules.checkpoint: Construct a truth table and trace at least three strings through a finite state machine.

modules.title: Graphs, trails and cycles
modules.definition: A graph G=(V,E) contains vertices and edges. Directed edges have orientation. An Eulerian trail uses every edge once; a Hamilton cycle visits every vertex once and returns to its start.
modules.equation: sum(deg(v), v in V) = 2|E|
modules.example: A connected undirected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree. A delivery route that must traverse every road is an edge-focused Euler problem; visiting every city once is vertex-focused and Hamiltonian.
modules.checkpoint: Do not confuse an Eulerian condition with a Hamiltonian condition.

modules.title: Connectivity and trees
modules.definition: A connected graph has a path between every pair of vertices. A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph; with n vertices it has exactly n-1 edges and a unique simple path between each pair.
modules.equation: For a tree: |E| = |V| - 1
modules.example: Removing any edge from a tree disconnects it, while adding any new edge creates exactly one cycle. These dual properties are useful when proving minimal connectivity.
modules.checkpoint: Prove the tree properties from connectedness and absence of cycles.

modules.title: Graph traversal and shortest paths
modules.definition: BFS explores by distance layers and gives shortest unweighted paths. DFS explores deeply before backtracking and supports connectivity, cycle detection, and ordering tasks. Weighted shortest paths require an algorithm whose assumptions match the edge weights.
modules.equation: BFS time = O(|V| + |E|)
modules.example: In an unweighted social graph, BFS from a profile discovers all profiles one connection away before those two connections away; the parent links reconstruct a shortest path.
modules.checkpoint: State whether the graph is directed, weighted, and allowed to contain negative weights before choosing an algorithm.

modules.title: Spanning trees, matching and assignment
modules.definition: A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex with minimum total edge weight. A matching contains edges with no shared endpoint. Job assignment is a weighted bipartite matching problem between workers and jobs.
modules.equation: MST has |V|-1 edges; assignment minimizes sum(c_ij x_ij)
modules.example: Kruskal's method repeatedly adds the lightest edge that does not create a cycle. In assignment, each worker and job must appear in exactly one selected pair.
modules.checkpoint: Explain why a locally light edge is safe before applying a greedy MST step.

modules.title: Network flows and transportation
topics: Optimal transportation through flows in networks
modules.definition: A flow network is a directed graph with capacities, a source, and a sink. A feasible flow respects capacity constraints and flow conservation. Maximum flow models transportation, routing, and allocation.
modules.equation: 0 <= f(u,v) <= c(u,v); inflow(v) = outflow(v)
modules.example: If two routes from source to sink have bottlenecks 5 and 3 and share no capacity, they can carry 8 units. An augmenting path increases flow by its smallest residual capacity.
modules.checkpoint: Check capacity, conservation, and residual edges after every augmentation.

courses.title: Advanced Computer Networks and Communication
courses.tagline: Connect physical transmission, network protocols, management, mobility, and security into one operational view.

modules.title: Telecommunications foundations
modules.definition: Telecommunication moves information over distance. Conducted media guides signals through copper or fiber; radiated media uses electromagnetic propagation. Bandwidth, attenuation, noise, delay, and signal-to-noise ratio shape achievable communication.
modules.equation: Shannon capacity: C = B log2(1 + S/N)
modules.example: Increasing bandwidth raises theoretical capacity, but noise and attenuation still limit reliable transmission. Fiber offers high bandwidth and low electromagnetic interference; radio supports mobility but shares spectrum.
modules.checkpoint: Compare a medium by bandwidth, reach, interference, mobility, cost, and security exposure.

modules.title: Coding, modulation and errors
modules.definition: Line and channel coding map information into transmitted symbols. Modulation varies a carrier. Detection adds redundancy to identify corruption; correction adds enough structured redundancy to recover some errors.
modules.equation: Hamming distance d_min detects up to d_min-1 errors and corrects floor((d_min-1)/2)
modules.example: A parity bit detects any odd number of flipped bits but cannot identify which bit changed. A CRC treats the bit string as a polynomial and checks a transmitted remainder.
modules.checkpoint: Distinguish source coding, channel coding, line coding, and modulation.

modules.title: Networks, standards and layered design
topics: LAN and WAN applications, hardware, and software
modules.definition: Layering separates concerns through services and protocols. The OSI model organizes communication into seven conceptual layers. Hubs, switches, routers, and gateways act at different scopes; standards allow independently built systems to interoperate.
modules.equation: End-to-end delay = processing + queueing + transmission + propagation
modules.example: A switch forwards frames within a LAN using link-layer addresses; a router forwards packets between networks using network-layer addresses.
modules.checkpoint: For any device or protocol, name its layer, inputs, outputs, and failure scope.

modules.title: Applications and system selection
topics: Selection of telecommunications and networking systems
modules.definition: Network design translates application requirements into topology, capacity, redundancy, manageability, security, and cost choices. Selection should follow measured requirements rather than brand preference.
modules.equation: Availability = uptime / total time
modules.example: A video service prioritizes throughput and jitter control; a transaction system prioritizes correctness, latency, availability, and secure recovery. A requirements matrix makes trade-offs visible.
modules.checkpoint: Record functional needs, service-level targets, risks, and total cost before selecting a system.

modules.title: Security, signatures and authentication
modules.definition: Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure, integrity detects alteration, and availability preserves service. Digital signatures bind a private-key operation to data; authentication protocols establish identity or possession of credentials.
modules.equation: signature = Sign(private_key, Hash(message))
modules.example: A verifier recomputes the message hash and verifies the signature with the public key. A nonce prevents an old authentication response from being replayed as fresh proof.
modules.checkpoint: Separate encryption from signatures and authentication from authorization.

modules.title: Wireless mobility
modules.definition: A WLAN connects devices over radio through access points or peer modes. Mobility introduces association, roaming, interference, and security concerns. Mobile IP preserves reachability as a node changes its point of attachment.
modules.equation: Effective wireless throughput < nominal link rate
modules.example: A roaming device may reassociate with a new access point while higher layers try to preserve sessions; congestion and interference can dominate performance even with a strong signal.
modules.checkpoint: Analyze mobility at link, network, transport, and application layers.

modules.title: SNMP models and proxying
topics: SNMP v1 and v2 organizational model
modules.definition: SNMP managers query or configure agents using managed objects defined in MIB modules. The information model names typed objects; the communication model exchanges protocol data units; the functional model covers monitoring and control. A proxy represents devices that cannot communicate directly with the manager.
modules.equation: managed object identifier = hierarchical OID
modules.example: A manager polls an interface counter, compares successive values, and estimates utilization. Traps or notifications report selected events without waiting for a poll.
modules.checkpoint: Explain manager, agent, MIB, OID, polling, notification, and proxy roles.

modules.title: Broadband, ATM and network management
modules.definition: ATM transports fixed-size cells through virtual connections. Operational management keeps inventory and configuration consistent, detects and isolates faults, and measures performance indicators such as latency, loss, throughput, and utilization.
modules.equation: utilization = observed traffic / link capacity
modules.example: A monitoring tool correlates rising interface errors with packet loss, while configuration history reveals whether a recent change preceded the fault.
modules.checkpoint: For each metric, define its unit, collection interval, baseline, and alert threshold.

modules.title: Web and XML management plus laboratory
topics: Programming protocols using C/C++ and MATLAB
modules.definition: Web-based management exposes operational views through browser-accessible interfaces. XML represents structured management data. Laboratory work connects protocol theory to parsers, sockets, traffic experiments, and numerical analysis.
modules.equation: goodput = useful application bits / elapsed time
modules.example: A lab can implement a client-server message exchange, inject controlled loss, measure round-trip time, and plot results in MATLAB while documenting protocol states.
modules.checkpoint: Every lab report should state topology, assumptions, procedure, raw observations, calculations, and limitations.

courses.title: Probability and Statistics
courses.tagline: Model uncertainty, simulate systems, and make defensible statistical inferences from data.

modules.title: Events and probability rules
modules.definition: A sample space contains possible outcomes and an event is a subset. Conditional probability updates the relevant sample space. Independence means one event does not change the probability of the other. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional probability using priors and evidence.
modules.equation: P(A|B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B); P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)
modules.example: If a detector is 95% sensitive, has 5% false positives, and prevalence is 1%, then a positive result has probability 0.0095/(0.0095+0.0495) about 16.1% of being a true case.
modules.checkpoint: Always define the sample space and distinguish P(A|B) from P(B|A).

modules.title: Random variables and discrete distributions
modules.definition: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. A probability mass function assigns probability to each discrete value. Each named distribution encodes a particular experiment and assumptions.
modules.equation: Binomial: P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k); Poisson: P(X=k)=e^(-lambda)lambda^k/k!
modules.example: Ten independent requests each fail with probability 0.1. The number of failures is Binomial(10,0.1), so P(no failures)=0.9^10.
modules.checkpoint: Match the story to assumptions: fixed trials, waiting time, or event count.

modules.title: Continuous distributions, expectation and CLT
modules.definition: A continuous density integrates to probability. Expectation summarizes a distribution's center; moments describe shape. The Central Limit Theorem explains why standardized sums or means often approach a normal distribution under suitable conditions.
modules.equation: E[X]=integral x f(x) dx; Z=(Xbar-mu)/(sigma/sqrt(n))
modules.example: If service times are exponential with rate 0.5 per minute, the mean is 2 minutes and P(X>4)=e^(-2). The CLT can approximate a mean of many independent service times.
modules.checkpoint: A density value is not itself a probability; integrate over an interval.

modules.title: Simulation and Monte Carlo
modules.definition: Simulation generates pseudo-random observations from a model. Monte Carlo estimates quantities by repeated sampling. Bootstrapping resamples observed data to approximate sampling variability when analytic formulas are difficult.
modules.equation: Monte Carlo estimate = (1/N) sum(g(X_i))
modules.example: Estimate pi by sampling N points uniformly in a unit square and multiplying the fraction inside the quarter circle by 4. Precision improves roughly with the square root of N.
modules.checkpoint: Report seed, number of runs, uncertainty, and convergence evidence.

modules.title: Stochastic processes
modules.definition: A stochastic process is a time-indexed family of random variables. Markov chains condition the future on the current state. Queuing systems combine arrival and service processes to study waiting and congestion.
modules.equation: Markov: P(X_(t+1)=j | history)=P(X_(t+1)=j | X_t=i)
modules.example: For a two-state up/down system, a transition matrix gives the chance of repair or failure per step. Multiplying a state distribution by the matrix advances it one step.
modules.checkpoint: State the index set, state space, transition assumptions, and whether time is discrete or continuous.

modules.title: Sampling, estimation and confidence intervals
modules.definition: A parameter describes a population; a statistic is computed from a sample. Estimation uses data to infer parameters. Method of moments matches sample and population moments; maximum likelihood chooses parameters that make observed data most plausible.
modules.equation: Xbar=(1/n)sum X_i; 95% large-sample CI: Xbar +/- 1.96 s/sqrt(n)
modules.example: A sample mean of 52 with s=10 and n=100 has approximate 95% interval 52 +/- 1.96, assuming conditions for the approximation are reasonable.
modules.checkpoint: Report estimator, assumptions, standard error, confidence level, and interpretation.

modules.title: Hypothesis testing and anomalies
topics: Type I and Type II errors
modules.definition: A hypothesis test measures how incompatible data are with a null model. Type I error rejects a true null; Type II error fails to reject a false null. Anomaly detection needs an explicit baseline and false-alarm trade-off.
modules.equation: power = 1 - beta; significance level = alpha
modules.example: At alpha=0.05, repeated testing across many independent metrics creates more opportunities for false positives, so multiplicity should be considered.
modules.checkpoint: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

modules.title: Exploration and statistical models
modules.definition: Exploratory graphics reveal distribution, relationships, and data quality. Least squares models a numeric response; logistic regression models log-odds for a binary response. ANOVA compares variation among and within groups. Robust and nonparametric methods reduce reliance on fragile assumptions.
modules.equation: least squares minimizes sum(y_i - yhat_i)^2; logit(p)=log(p/(1-p))
modules.example: Plot residuals after regression: curvature suggests missing structure, while widening spread suggests non-constant variance. A coefficient must be interpreted with units and other predictors held constant.
modules.checkpoint: Inspect data and residuals before trusting a fitted model.

courses.title: Pattern Recognition
courses.tagline: Learn representations and decision rules from experience, then evaluate what generalizes.

modules.title: Learning problems and models
modules.definition: Learning uses experience to improve performance on a defined task. The output may be a label, function, relation, grammar, probability model, value estimate, behavior, or program. A sound formulation identifies input representation, target, loss, data source, and evaluation protocol.
modules.equation: empirical risk = (1/n) sum L(f(x_i), y_i)
modules.example: Document recognition maps an image or token sequence to a label. The same data could instead support probability estimation, structured parsing, or a learned decision policy.
modules.checkpoint: Define task, experience, performance measure, and generalization target.

modules.title: Bayesian, MAP and MDL frameworks
modules.definition: Bayesian inference combines prior belief and likelihood into a posterior. MAP selects the parameter with highest posterior density. MDL favors the model that gives the shortest combined description of model and data.
modules.equation: posterior proportional to likelihood x prior; theta_MAP=argmax p(D|theta)p(theta)
modules.example: With limited data, a prior can stabilize parameter estimates. As data accumulate, the likelihood often dominates. MDL penalizes complexity when it does not compress the observations enough.
modules.checkpoint: State priors and model assumptions; do not present MAP as prior-free.

modules.title: Parameter estimation and model families
modules.definition: Parameter estimation fits a chosen model family. A sufficient statistic preserves all sample information relevant to a parameter under the model. Trees partition feature space, neural networks compose learned transformations, SVMs maximize a margin, and Bayesian networks encode conditional dependence.
modules.equation: SVM margin is proportional to 1/||w||
modules.example: For a Bernoulli model, the number of successes is sufficient for the success probability. A decision tree split can be chosen by impurity reduction, then validated on unseen data.
modules.checkpoint: Compare interpretability, capacity, optimization, data needs, and calibration.

modules.title: Text and sequence models
modules.definition: Bag of words represents token counts while discarding order. N-grams preserve short local context. Markov models assume limited state dependence; hidden Markov models infer unobserved states from observed emissions. Relational models include dependencies among entities.
modules.equation: P(w_1...w_T) approximately product P(w_t | previous n-1 words)
modules.example: A bigram model estimates a word from its predecessor. In an HMM for document zones, hidden states might be title, paragraph, and caption while observations are visual or textual features.
modules.checkpoint: Identify what information is lost by the independence or Markov assumption.

modules.title: Instance, rule and ensemble methods
modules.definition: Association rules describe co-occurrence patterns using support and confidence. Nearest-neighbour methods predict from nearby training examples. Local regression fits around a query point. Ensembles combine diverse learners to reduce error.
modules.equation: confidence(A -> B)=support(A union B)/support(A)
modules.example: In k-nearest neighbours, feature scaling changes distance and therefore neighbours. A validation set can choose k; test data must remain untouched until final evaluation.
modules.checkpoint: Check leakage, scaling, distance choice, diversity, and validation design.

modules.title: Computational learning theory
modules.definition: Learning theory relates hypothesis complexity, data volume, errors, accuracy, and confidence. VC dimension measures the largest set a hypothesis class can shatter. Occam-style reasoning controls complexity; boosting combines weak learners into a stronger classifier.
modules.equation: generalization bounds commonly grow with complexity and shrink with sample size
modules.example: A more expressive classifier may fit training data better yet need more observations to guarantee similar test performance. Boosting repeatedly emphasizes misclassified cases.
modules.checkpoint: Separate training error from a claim about unseen-data error.

modules.title: Representation, reduction and visualization
modules.definition: Feature selection retains a subset of original variables. Dimensionality reduction maps data to a smaller representation. Visualization supports exploration but a two-dimensional projection can distort global or local structure.
modules.equation: PCA chooses directions maximizing projected variance
modules.example: Standardize differently scaled features before PCA when scale should not dominate. Fit the transformation on training data only, then apply it to validation and test data.
modules.checkpoint: Treat a visualization as evidence to investigate, not automatic proof of separable classes.

modules.title: Clustering and mixture models
modules.definition: Clustering groups observations without supplied labels. K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance to centroids. Hierarchical methods build nested merges or splits. Mixture models view observations as arising from latent component distributions.
modules.equation: k-means objective = sum_i ||x_i - mu_(cluster(i))||^2
modules.example: Different initial centroids can give different k-means solutions, so use multiple starts and report stability. A Gaussian mixture gives soft membership probabilities rather than only hard labels.
modules.checkpoint: Justify distance, scaling, cluster count, and evaluation method.

modules.title: Document recognition application
modules.definition: Document recognition integrates preprocessing, segmentation, representation, classification or sequence modeling, and evaluation. Errors can propagate across stages, so component and end-to-end metrics are both useful.
modules.equation: F1 = 2 precision recall / (precision + recall)
modules.example: A system may deskew a scan, detect text regions, recognize characters, reconstruct reading order, and compare output with ground truth using character or word error rate.
modules.checkpoint: Document data provenance, train-test separation, class imbalance, and representative failure cases.

courses.title: Research Methodology
courses.tagline: Move from a defensible question to ethical evidence, analysis, interpretation, and publication.

modules.title: Foundations and language of research
modules.definition: Research is systematic inquiry designed to produce defensible knowledge. Deduction tests consequences derived from theory; induction develops patterns or theory from observations. Concepts become measurable through explicit operational definitions and variables.
modules.equation: question -> design -> evidence -> analysis -> interpretation -> communication
modules.example: The construct 'system usability' is not directly observed; a study must define indicators, instruments, and scoring before collecting evidence.
modules.checkpoint: Write one conceptual definition and one operational definition for every key construct.

modules.title: Problem identification and hypotheses
modules.definition: A research problem identifies a knowledge gap; a research question makes it answerable. A hypothesis states a testable expectation. The null provides a reference model, while the alternative represents the competing claim.
modules.equation: H0: parameter = reference; H1: parameter differs or follows a stated direction
modules.example: Question: Does interface A reduce task time compared with B? H0 states no difference in the population; H1 states a difference. The design must define users, tasks, timing, and exclusions.
modules.checkpoint: A useful hypothesis is specific, measurable, falsifiable, and connected to theory.

modules.title: Research design
modules.definition: Research design is the plan connecting questions to evidence and inference. Exploratory designs clarify poorly understood problems; descriptive designs characterize populations or phenomena; experiments manipulate an independent variable and observe outcomes under controlled comparison.
modules.equation: observed effect = treatment effect + bias + random variation
modules.example: A randomized experiment estimates the effect of a new interface on completion time. A descriptive survey can estimate current adoption but alone cannot establish the same causal claim.
modules.checkpoint: Align question, sampling, measurement, comparison, analysis, and validity threats.

modules.title: Qualitative and quantitative approaches
modules.definition: Qualitative research investigates meaning and context through rich evidence; quantitative research analyzes measured variables numerically. Mixed approaches integrate them when neither alone answers the full question.
modules.equation: triangulation compares evidence from multiple methods or sources
modules.example: Interviews can reveal why users abandon a tool, while logs estimate how often and at which step. Integration connects themes with observed behavioral patterns.
modules.checkpoint: Choose methods because they answer the question, not because one label sounds more rigorous.

modules.title: Measurement quality and levels
modules.definition: Validity concerns whether an inference or instrument measures what it claims. Reliability concerns consistency. Nominal values are categories, ordinal values have order, interval scales have equal differences, and ratio scales also have a meaningful zero.
modules.equation: observed score = true component + measurement error
modules.example: A 1-to-5 satisfaction item is ordered, but equal spacing between responses is an assumption. Repeating an unreliable instrument cannot repair poor construct validity.
modules.checkpoint: Name the scale level before choosing summaries or statistical tests.

modules.title: Sampling
topics: Population, sample, frame, error, size, and non-response
modules.definition: A target population is the group of interest; the sampling frame is the operational list used to select units. Probability sampling gives known selection mechanisms. Sample size depends on precision, variability, design, analysis, and practical constraints.
modules.equation: SE of a mean decreases approximately as 1/sqrt(n)
modules.example: Stratified sampling can ensure representation from small but important groups. Increasing sample size does not remove coverage bias or systematic non-response.
modules.checkpoint: Document target population, frame coverage, selection method, response, and exclusions.

modules.title: Data preparation and analysis
modules.definition: Data preparation applies a documented codebook, type checks, missing-value rules, and quality checks. Univariate analysis summarizes one variable. Cross-tabulation and the chi-square test assess association between categorical variables under appropriate assumptions.
modules.equation: chi-square = sum((observed-expected)^2/expected)
modules.example: For device type by completion status, compute expected counts from row and column totals, inspect whether counts are adequate, calculate chi-square, and report effect context rather than only significance.
modules.checkpoint: Preserve raw data, make transformations reproducible, and distinguish missing from zero.

modules.title: Interpretation and paper writing
modules.definition: Interpretation connects results to the research question, assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and prior work. A paper typically communicates problem, related context, methods, results, discussion, and references. Venue selection should consider scope, audience, review quality, policies, and fit rather than a metric alone.
modules.equation: claim strength must not exceed design and evidence strength
modules.example: An observational association should not be written as a causal effect. Reusing substantial prior text or results without transparent citation can be self-plagiarism.
modules.checkpoint: Audit every claim for evidence, uncertainty, attribution, and reproducibility.

modules.title: Research sources and databases
modules.definition: Reference works orient a topic and supply terminology; research databases help discover primary literature. Search should combine concepts, synonyms, Boolean operators, filters, citation chaining, and a documented inclusion process.
modules.equation: search concept blocks: (termA OR synonym) AND (termB OR synonym)
modules.example: Begin with a broad scoping search, refine keywords from relevant papers, then trace references backward and citations forward while recording queries and dates.
modules.checkpoint: A reproducible search records database, exact query, date, filters, and screening criteria.

modules.title: Research tools and techniques
modules.definition: Reference managers store metadata and attachments and generate citations, but records still require verification. Document tools support structured writing and revision. Similarity tools flag overlap for human review; they do not determine plagiarism by themselves.
modules.equation: tool output + researcher judgment + transparent process = defensible workflow
modules.example: Import a DOI into a reference manager, verify author and venue metadata, attach the lawful full text, tag the study, cite it through the chosen style, and check the final bibliography.
modules.checkpoint: Back up the library, verify metadata, preserve notes, and never treat a similarity score as a verdict.
